welcome to section 8 of neurology in this section we'll be discussing seizures let's get started here's our overview slide let's begin by discussing some basic principles seizure is defined as abnormal electrical activity of the brain that results from hyperexcitability of neurons this can be partial which refers to the fact that only one part of the brain is affected or generalized which refers to the fact that the entire brain is affected seizures can be caused by genetic and structural brain abnormalities metabolic abnormalities such as severe hypoglycemia can also cause seizures other causes include tumors infection trauma and stroke manifestations depend on the location of the abnormal activity and whether it affects one side or both sides of the brain seizures can be provoked by a lack of sleep stress and excessive alcohol consumption all right now let's dive into the specific types of seizures beginning with partial seizures before we jump in let's take a look at this overview diagram notice that seizures are broken up into several categories first those that involve one hemisphere and those that involve both if only one hemisphere is involved it's called a partial or focal seizure so partial seizures are those that affect a single area of the brain or are confined to only one side of the brain they're also called focal seizures partial seizures are most commonly caused by a structural brain abnormality that likely leads to the electrical imbalances in the brain the temporal lobe is the most common lobe involved in partial though all lobes can be affected patients may experience an aura prior to the seizure onset an aura is characterized by sensory or psychiatric symptoms that can occur before the onset of the seizure examples of auras include experiencing fear deja vu or seeing bright lights because the seizure is focal or affects only one side of the brain symptoms therefore usually only occur on one side of the body usually contralateral to the affected side of the brain so for example if the left brain is affected the right arm or right leg may be involved in the seizure partial seizures are described according to whether there is an impairment of consciousness and there are two types of partial seizures simple or complex so if we return to this diagram we can see simple and complex with simple partial seizures consciousness is not impaired so no impaired consciousness with complex partial seizures the consciousness is impaired so yes it's difficult to assess impairment of consciousness during the seizure episode the easiest way is to ask the patient afterwards whether they remember what had happened if patients can recall the episode then their consciousness was likely intact and they had a simple partial seizure another point to consider is the presence of a fever if the focal seizure is thought to have been caused by a fever then the diagnosis is a complex febrile seizure it's important to note that seizures can start out as partial or focal in one side of the brain and spread to the other side of the brain resulting in a generalized seizure this progression is called a secondary generalized seizure so to review a simple partial seizure is a focal seizure where consciousness remains intact symptoms vary depending on the affected region this includes motor sensory autonomic and psychic symptoms motor symptoms include repetitive muscle movements or jerks an interesting series of motor symptoms can occur when the abnormal electrical activity spreads to adjacent areas of the brain this is called jacksonian march as the symptoms march and progressively involve other muscle groups some presenting sensory symptoms may include vertigo olfactory symptoms or tingling finally other manifestations include autonomic changes such as sweating or flushing and psychic symptoms such as fear and hallucinations as we just discussed the second type of partial seizure is called complex seizures a complex partial seizure describes focal seizures during which consciousness is impaired the patients may also experience automatisms which are unconscious repetitive movements that have no purpose examples include lip smacking chewing or swallowing finally a complex febrile seizure is similar to a complex partial seizure but the cause is due to a fever this is a picture of a two-month-old boy demonstrating the asymmetrical tonic limb posture right here the asymmetrical limb involvement indicates a partial seizure this position is also called the fencing position all right now let's try a girl does not recall having the episode this indicates a complex seizure since consciousness was impaired so this all points towards the most likely type of seizure being a complex partial seizure remember that complex partial seizures are focal seizures where the consciousness is impaired okay now that we've discussed partial seizures let's move on to discuss generalized seizures generalized seizures involve both hemispheres and there are many types you can see many of them listed here unlike a partial seizure which may only involve one side of the body generalized seizures involve both hemispheres and therefore produce abnormalities affecting the body bilaterally tonic colonic seizure is the most common type of generalized seizure it consists of alternating between the tonic phase which is characterized by stiffening or rigidity of the body and the clonic phase which is characterized by uncontrolled repetitive muscle movements seizures can also present with only tonic or clonic phases myoclonic seizures present with rapid repetitive muscle jerks these are rhythmic meaning there is no pattern to the movements this is in contrast to clonic seizures which are characterized by rhythmic movements of the muscles atonic seizures are characterized by a loss of muscle tone causing the patient to drop to the floor it's therefore dangerous as it can lead to severe falls and injuries though it's often confused with fainting to differentiate these remember that seizures can lead to loss of bladder and bowel control as well as tongue biting which are not associated with fainting absence seizures are a type of generalized seizure that presents with brief episodes of blank stares they're typically not preceded by an aura or a post-ictal state meaning there is no confusion after the seizure passes they can occur many times throughout the day of son's seizure is most commonly present in children and can disrupt their school performance and teachers will remark that the child stares into the distance frequently on eeg a classic finding that can be described is the presence of three hertz spike and wave complexes finally absance seizures are treated with ethosuccsimide before we move on let's briefly mention simple febrile seizures this is a generalized seizure that is caused by a fever and is most commonly tonic clonic in nature so by generalized we mean that it involves both sides of the brain and causes movement throughout the limbs bilaterally and by tonic clonic we mean that there is alterations between body stiffness and uncontrolled repetitive muscle movements all right now let's talk about epilepsy from the overview slide notice the asterisk next to both partial and generalized seizures if either of these are recurrent or unprovoked the diagnosis of epilepsy can be made so epilepsy is a disorder of chronic recurrent and unprovoked seizures unprovoked seizures refers to seizures that are not caused by identifiable factors such as lack of sleep tumors or trauma status epilepticus is a critical condition that can occur in patients with epilepsy it's defined as a single seizure lasting five or more minutes or the presence of recurrent seizures without regaining consciousness in between it's important to recognize that this is an emergency and the treatment is iv benzodiazepines all right now let's finish up by discussing differences fever and hyperthermia here is a table that summarizes the most important differences let's start with fever fever is defined as the increase in body temperature more than the normal daily variation the hypothalamus responds to the cytokines by increasing the basal temperature of the body resulting in a fever fever is most commonly caused by infection or inflammation the body temperature during fever is usually less than 40 degrees celsius and it can be treated with antipyretics such as nsaids or acetaminophen to block the cytokines that act on the hypothalamus the underlying cause of the fever should also be treated for example antibiotics can be given to treat an underlying infection the fever is usually resolved by treating the underlying cause fever can cause febrile seizures especially in children but this is generally considered benign hyperthermia on the other hand is an increase in body temperature that exceeds the body's ability to dissipate heat due to either external or internal sources of heat an example of an external source is a heat stroke due to an extremely hot environment internal sources include medications that can cause serotonin syndrome or metabolic diseases hyperthermia can raise the body temperature to above 40 degrees celsius the management is different than fever as this includes the rapid reduction of body temperature via physical means such as cool baths and iv rehydration the use of cooling blankets however is not recommended as this can lead to excessive vasoconstriction and decrease heat loss hyperthermia can be rapidly fatal that's why it's important to recognize and treat it promptly it can cause a wide range of organ dysfunction including ards arrhythmia neurologic dysfunction and multi-organ failure all right now that we've covered the information let's review with the final question a nine-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents due to inattention his parents myoclonic seizure all right hopefully from the question stem you notice that this child is frequently found staring into the distance he also is inattentive and has declining academic performance throughout the lecture broadly speaking you should recognize that there are two major types of errors intrinsic errors and extrinsic errors intrinsic errors of morphogenesis can be defined by the failure of the embryo to develop due to abnormal genes or other internal processes examples of intrinsic errors include agenesis aplasia hypoplasia and malformation which we'll discuss in a moment extrinsic errors are external factors within the womb that disrupt normal development in other words it's not the developing embryo that's causing the air it's something external to the embryo examples of extrinsic errors include deformation and disruption all right with this background let's discuss intrinsic errors first and then we'll move on to discuss extrinsic errors the first intrinsic error we'll discuss is agenesis agenesis is defined as an absent organ due to absent primordial tissue a great example of this is renal agenesis this is a defect in the fetus which results in absent kidney development because the kidneys are essential for amniotic fluid production less amniotic fluid is produced which is also called oligohydramnios the fetus is compressed due to less surrounding fluid which creates a sequence of complications known as potter sequence some of the findings include pulmonary hyperplasia flat faces club feet and wrinkly skin we discussed this in much more detail in renal embryology next is aplasia aplasia is an absent organ despite the presence of primordial tissue this is different from a genesis because there is no primordial tissue present in agenesis whereas in aplasia there is an example of aplasia is degeorge syndrome which is aplasia of the thymus this is due to failure of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches to develop and it results in thymic parathyroid and cardiac defects it also results in abnormal faces which is pictured here on the right next is hypoplasia hypoplasia is underdevelopment or incomplete development of an organ or tissue our example of hypoplasia is klinefelter syndrome which is characterized by an extra x chromosome in males resulting in 46xy this results in testicular hypoplasia or small testes reduced size or incomplete development of the testes results in low testosterone which gives the affected patient a more feminine appearance including an increased amount of breast tissue and less body hair the last intrinsic error of morphogenesis which we'll discuss is malformation a malformation is an intrinsic disruption that occurs when a structure is not formed partially formed or abnormally formed during embryonic development this occurs during weeks three to eight holoprosencephaly is an example of this we discuss this disease in depth in our neuroembryology video but briefly this is a defect of forebrain development that results in midline defects and cns deformities it presents on a spectrum of severity with the most severe form resulting in cyclopia pictured here off to the right notice that in this disease the patient has a single eye in the midline region right here okay now that we've finished talking about intrinsic errors let's move on to extrinsic errors the first error is deformation deformation is defined as an abnormality of the position of body parts due to extrinsic intrauterine mechanical forces unlike malformation which occurs during the embryonic period deformation occurs after the embryonic period an example of this is when a mother has a septate or bicornuate uterus and this can result in compression of the fetus and a flattened skull last but not least we have disruption disruption is defined as secondary breakdown of a previously normal tissue or structure it can result from a vascular or mechanical process that leads to tissue compromise a classic example of this is amniotic band sequence or abs this is a rare condition that occurs when strands of amniotic sac get entangled among the fetus's digits causing them to lose circulation via formation of constrictive rings which then results in the development of limb defects off to the right we can see an example of this right here notice that the fingers are much smaller than normal all right now that we've covered the type of errors let's review with the practice question a three-day-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother due to difficulty feeding she is worried that he is starving and nothing she does helps him feed better on physical examination the newborn is well appearing but is found to have a cleft palate what type of error of morphogenesis best describes this patient's presentation a a genesis b aplasia c hypoplasia d malformation or e deformation okay hopefully from the question sent me notice that this is pretty straightforward and what type of malformation do we categorize a cleft palate a cleft palate occurs when a structure is partially or abnormally formed and is a midline defect this falls into the category of malformation so d is the correct answer a genesis and aplasia are incorrect because there is no organ missing hypoplasia is incorrect because again all organs appear to have developed normally and there is no mention of underdevelopment but rather abnormal development in other words i like to think of hypoplasia as not growing enough whereas malformation means it grew but in an altered way so again c is incorrect finally deformation is incorrect because deformations are due to extrinsic forces while a cleft palate is an intrinsic force so again the correct answer is d malformation and with that we've covered everything you need to know regarding errors of morphogenesis

welcome to section 4 of embryology in this section we'll be discussing left to right shunts let's get started left right shunts occur when blood from the systemic arterial circulation mixes with the systemic venous blood these include conditions like ventricular septal defects atrial septal defects and patent ductus arteriosus a key distinction between left to right shunts and right to left shunts is that newborns are acyonotic but cyanosis can present many years later this is because a left to right shunt results in oxygenated blood going back to the deoxygenated side of the heart therefore deoxygenated blood is not entering the systemic circulation at least not initially over time however left to right shunts may reverse and this process of shunt reversal is known as eisenmanger syndrome and is a potential complication of left to right shunts let's talk about this in a bit more detail and then we'll go through the three left to right shunts so here we have two drawings of the heart the left image will represent early in the course of a left to right shunt and the right image will represent what will happen later on so early and late let's say this patient was born with an atrial septal defect or asd which we can see right here the pressures on the left side of the heart are normally much greater than the right side of the heart this is because the left side of the heart must pump against the entire resistance of the systemic vasculature whereas the right side of the heart only has to pump against the resistance of the pulmonary vasculature so the blood flows the path of least resistance and in this patient with an asd the blood goes from the left atrium to the right atrium so now we'll focus our attention on the image on the right which represents late the excess blood on the right side of the heart can enter the pulmonary circulation and the fluid overload in the pulmonary vasculature can cause arterial remodeling and increased pulmonary vascular resistance so increased resistance because the right ventricle now has to pump against more resistance the pressure on the right side of the heart increases and the right ventricle attempts to adapt via hypertrophy eventually the pressure on the right side of the heart becomes greater than the left side of the heart which can lead to reversal of the shunt and then a patient will develop a right to left shunt so the pressure over here is less than the right side of the heart and we get blood flowing from the right atrium into the left atrium this is problematic because now we have deoxygenated blood going from the right side of the heart directly to the left side of the heart and then into the tissues so again eisenmanger syndrome occurs when a chronic left to right shunt but also have episodes of hyperactivity and impulsivity to diagnose adhd in kids under 17 there must be a pattern of behavior that is consistently positive for both types of symptoms in at least two different settings so for example a child may have episodes of excessive talking and interrupting others at school and then exhibits the same behavior at home this idea of exhibiting the symptoms in two different settings is important for the diagnosis this behavior must be present for at least six months and it must begin prior to age 12. another important point is that the symptoms must be disproportionate for the developmental stage of the individual this is significant because it may be normal for children under 17 to have many of the symptoms listed in the dsm criteria for example a child may disrupt others talking on the phone which could be normal for a three-year-old however this would be abnormal for a 16 year old this is why it may be possible that there has been a recent uptick in over-diagnosing adhd regardless the key feature is that the behavior must truly be excessive for the stage of development and that it is consistently interfering with normal daily functioning a major key to all psychiatric illnesses is the element of impaired functionality and adhd is no exception in the case of adhd the symptoms must be causing such effects as poor school performance so academic abnormally high levels of stress due to the inability to focus or an inability to get along with others so social alright so that was adhd and kids now let's discuss adhd in adults first it's important to know that the diagnostic criteria for children and adults are similar so both adults and children have to experience multiple symptoms in two or more settings for a six month period that disrupts functionality however adolescents and adults over the age of 17 can be tricky to diagnose because some of the hyperactive and impulsive symptoms tend to diminish with age for example an adult with adhd probably won't have as much trouble staying seated for longer periods of time but still might talk excessively constantly fidget or make impulsive decisions like quitting a job without another option or ending a relationship without fully thinking it over on the other hand the symptoms of inattention often persist throughout adulthood and these can cause significant problems at work or in other settings due to difficulties creating organizing and completing tasks or goals the inability to remain focused on a certain task meet deadlines and overlooked mistakes can cause notable distress and dysfunction one of the keys to diagnosing an adult is by obtaining a thorough history because the hyperactive and intensive symptoms described need to have been present since childhood so prior to age 12. finally adults with adhd are often described as irritable or anxious and they are at an increased risk for mood disorders and substance abuse due to the effects of their illness or impulsive decisions that lead them to substance abuse alright let's review what we've covered so far with a question a 24 year old male began working at a new job four === FILE: Renal pathology 2 [TBzSIYA6ZD0].txt ===

 Welcome to section 2 of renal pathology, in this section we'll be discussing chronic renal failure, let's get started. In this lecture we'll be covering the basic principles, the causes and features and treatment of chronic renal failure. Let's start with the basic principles. Chronic renal failure is the gradual irreversible decline in kidney function. This decline in renal function leads to excess retained nitrogenous waste products and electrolyte disturbances. In other words, electrolytes and toxins that are normally secreted from the body will build up in the serum. This can lead to a variety of systemic complications seen in chronic renal failure. Next, let's discuss the causes of chronic renal failure. Many insults to the kidney may lead to chronic renal failure if they happen over time. And keep in mind that the insults I'm referring to are primarily responsible for causing acute renal failure. But over time, they may progress to chronic renal failure, especially if the acute renal failure is not treated properly. Glomerular diseases, like focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and membranous nephropathy, disrupt normal kidney filtration and may progress to chronic renal failure. Other, more common causes of chronic renal failure are diabetes and hypertension. Let's focus first on diabetes. Diabetes mellitus is a state of hyperglycemia. And hyperglycemia leads to non-enzymatic glycosylation of the vascular basement membrane. And this glycosylation, or sugar, getting added to the basement membrane of the vasculature, results in hyaline arteriosclerosis. And the vessels we're referring to specifically are the afferent and efferent arterioles of the kidney. This sclerosis eventually leads to hyperfiltration. Here's an image of the glomerulus with the afferent and efferent arterioles labeled. In diabetes, as I mentioned, hyaline sclerosis can affect these vessels. However, this hyaline arteriosclerosis affects the efferent arterioles more than the afferent arterioles. Remember from physiology that constriction or narrowing of the efferent arterioles will decrease kidney blood flow. So that means there's an increase in blood being filtered and entering the glomerulus. So there's increased filtration pressure. Another way of saying this is that there's an increase in GFR leading to hyperfiltration. And that hyperfiltration leads to irreversible damage to the nephrons, which is what causes chronic renal failure. So now we've discussed how diabetes works in causing chronic renal failure, but how does hypertension cause any problems? Well, hypertension causes blood vessels of the kidney to harden and narrow. This means that the nephrons are unable to receive oxygen and nutrients. This leads to a decrease in filtration, or hypofiltration. So you could think of hypofiltration as essentially damaging the nephron through starving it of the oxygen and nutrients that it needs. Whereas hyperfiltration, like we discussed in diabetes, damages the nephron by overworking it. Next, let's discuss the features of chronic renal failure. Chronic renal failure can lead to many issues, and we've listed them on this slide. Uremia results from increased nitrogenous waste products in the body. It presents with nausea, anorexia, pericarditis, platelet dysfunction, encephalopathy with asterixis, and deposition of urea crystals in the skin. And this skin finding is often called uremic frost. I want to point out why asterixis occurs. Well, this is a tremor of the hand when the wrist is extended, and it resembles a bird's flapping wings. So if you have somebody's arms out straight and their wrist fully extended, so they're looking at the back of their hand, then the wrist will be flapping. Now, the sodium and water retention can lead to several problems. For example, sodium and water retention congests the heart and prevents the heart from working properly, which can lead to heart failure. And if the heart is unable to pump efficiently, blood can back up into the lungs, eventually leading to pulmonary edema. Lastly, by causing extra strain on the blood vessels, sodium and water retention can lead to hypertension. In chronic renal failure, potassium is not properly excreted from the kidneys, which can lead to a buildup of potassium in the serum, or hyperkalemia. Metabolic acidosis occurs due to a combination of two main problems, impaired ammonium excretion, which means more acidic serum, and also because the kidneys aren't functioning properly, there is decreased bicarbonate formation, which you'd normally expect and need in the renal tubules. Lastly, the kidneys are often unable to make urethropoietin, or EPO. This can lead to anemia. Now let's talk about renal osteodystrophy. This is another complication of chronic renal failure. Here's the underlying pathophysiology here. There's hyperphosphatemia, because the kidneys are unable to excrete phosphate the way it needs to. There's hypocalcemia, because the kidneys are unable to reabsorb calcium the way it needs to. And there's failure of vitamin D hydroxylation, because the kidney is not able to activate vitamin D. This can lead to secondary hyperparathyroidism. And if left untreated, this can progress to tertiary hyperparathyroidism. And with that hyperparathyroidism, we're basically saying there's elevated PTH. And that can lead to hypercalcemia and subperiosteal thinning of the bones. The thyroid gland is shown here. And posterior to this gland are the parathyroid glands, which release PTH, which then stimulates the bone, which you can see labeled here. And it causes the bone then to release calcium into the serum. PTH will also stimulate the intestines, which you can see on the right, causing it to absorb more calcium from the gut, which of course leads to increased serum calcium. Now, PTH also stimulates the kidneys, here in the middle, to reabsorb serum calcium. Also convert vitamin D to its most active form. And excrete phosphate. Normally, high serum calcium, low serum phosphate, and even high vitamin D can negatively feed back and inhibit the release of PTH. However, in chronic renal failure, the kidneys are damaged and can't perform these functions. This leads to a decrease in serum calcium, decreased active vitamin D, and increased serum phosphate. These signal to the parathyroid gland to release PTH. So PTH will be high. Despite the increased PTH, the kidneys are still unable to respond to the PTH. After all, they're failing. However, the bones will still respond to all the PTH, so the bones will release their calcium. However, this can cause problems over time, because the bones need calcium to remain strong. So the chronic loss of calcium can lead to bone loss with subperiosteal thinning. So as we've described, there's lots of issues because of the kidneys not working, which leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism. In other words, lots of PTH. This may present with bone pain, because remember, there's subperiosteal thinning. And if this is poorly managed or left untreated, it can actually progress to tertiary hyperparathyroidism. This is a condition in which the parathyroid glands no longer respond to high calcium levels. So this means that even when the calcium is high, the parathyroid glands will continually secrete PTH. So there's persistently high PTH. This will stimulate the bones to continually release calcium, causing hypercalcemia, and obviously subperiosteal thinning of the bones. So how do you treat chronic renal failure? Well, chronic renal failure is treated with dialysis. It's important to note that dialysis can actually lead to the development of cysts with shrunken kidneys. And this feature can actually increase the risk of renal cell carcinoma. In addition to dialysis, chronic renal failure often requires a renal transplant. Let's try a question to wrap up this lecture. A 57-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency room with nausea, vomiting, chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, and dizziness. His chest pain has been present for two to three days and is described as burning and worse on inspiration. On physical examination, his skin is pale with numerous areas of bruising. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral rails. Chest x-ray shows moderate cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings. Assuming the parathyroid glands are still able to respond appropriately to serum calcium, what are the most likely serum findings in this patient? A, low PTH, low calcium, low phosphate, and low vitamin D. B, increased blood pH. C, increased PTH, decreased calcium, increased phosphate, and decreased vitamin D. Or D, increased erythropoietin concentration. So this man presents with dyspnea, chest pain that's burning, and he's also got rails, and he's also got cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings. What does that tell us? It tells us that he has pulmonary edema. He also presents with nausea and vomiting and platelet dysfunction. At least that's what we're thinking right now because of the numerous areas of bruising. Now, if you were thinking about tertiary hyperparathyroidism, you might have been expecting the calcium level to be elevated. However, we aren't suspecting this because in this question stem, we're specifically told that it's likely to be a serum calcium.  undertaking  and the capillaries within the glomerulus. That causes enlarged pores between the podocytes. And remember that podocytes link together to form a barrier. And that barrier prevents large molecules and other essential substances from being filtered into the urine. And if the pores between the podocytes become large, then this will lead to the leakage of red blood cells, as well as proteins and electrolytes. And the kidney responds to this loss by constricting blood vessels, which actually ends up leading to a decrease in GFR. And this causes the retention of nitrogenous waste and retention of creatinine, as well as salt and water. Here's an image of a cross-section of a glomerulus. Notice the capillaries right here, lined by endothelial cells, with the afferent arteriole representing the blood that comes in and the efferent arteriole representing the blood that leaves. As I mentioned on the previous slide, in nephritic syndrome, there's inflammation. And this causes these capillaries to swell. You can imagine that this swelling would cause the attached podocytes, which you can see here, would end up pulling apart. So these pores you see would actually become larger, because the podocytes are pushed away from one another as the capillaries swell. So this allows large molecules to fit through. Now let's talk about the clinical findings in nephritic syndrome. Nephritic syndrome presents with limited proteinuria, which is less than 3.5 grams per day. This differentiates nephritic syndrome from nephrotic syndrome. In nephrotic syndrome, there's greater than 3.5 grams of protein found in the urine per day. Nephritic syndrome also presents with salt retention. This retention of salt leads to periorbital edema and hypertension. And since those pores are so large, red blood cells can actually fit through and enter the urine, causing hematuria. And you'd see dysmorphic red blood cells in the urine because they're squeezing through the podocytes and becoming dysmorphic. And once they enter the tubular lumen, they can form casts, which you can see on your analysis. Now, nephritic syndrome may also lead to acute kidney injury, which you would tell based on decreased urine output, or oliguria, decreased GFR, or increased serum BUN, or increased creatinine. But it doesn't always cause this. So I emphasize that it may lead to this. Let's move on to the causes. The four main causes of nephritic syndrome, which you see over here, are acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, which is also known as Berger disease, and Alport syndrome. And when you think of nephritic syndromes, remember inflamed capillaries, and proteinuria of less than 3.5 grams per day. And when it presents in adults, it may progress to acute kidney injury. And sometimes, in adults or children, it may progress rapidly to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. And we'll discuss that later in this lecture, as you can see with this bottom row, where we discuss rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Now, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis normally presents with hematuria 2 to 3 weeks after an infection. And there's also decreased C3 protein, as well as decreased total complement protein levels. And that's because they're consumed during the inflammation, because inflammation causes the activation of the complement system. So C3 is used up in an attempt to fight whatever the body perceives to be an infection. So this leads to some interesting findings when you look at the biopsy. On electron microscopy, we see subepithelial humps. And on immunofluorescence, we can see this granular appearance. Okay, let's move on to IgA nephropathy. This is often called Berger disease. And this is the most common cause of nephropathy worldwide. And it's caused by IgA immune complex deposition in the mesangium of the glomeruli. So IgA in the mesangium. And this presents with episodic gross or microscopic hematuria, and typically in childhood. Another important feature is that it's usually seen days after a mucosal infection. Remember from immunology that IgA is the antibody responsible for fighting infections found in the mucosal areas, like the gut and respiratory tract.  N-19-19- Nephrolithiasis, more commonly known as kidney stones, is the deposition of urinary solute, which then forms a calculus, or stone. Now what are the risk factors for developing a kidney stone? There are two main risk factors associated with developing nephrolithiasis. First, patients that have a high solute concentration in their urine are at an increased risk of developing nephrolithiasis. This is because when the concentration of solutes is increased, then the solute is more likely to precipitate and form crystals. For example, patients with increased urinary calcium concentration, also known as hypercalciuria, are at an increased risk for developing calcium oxalate stones because the calcium precipitates out of the urine. And we'll talk about the types of stones more in a minute. The second risk factor is low urinary volume. For example, in a patient with dehydration, this is also tied to the high solute concentration idea because a low urinary volume means the concentration of the solute is increased, and so that will increase the risk of stone precipitation. Now let's talk about the presentation of kidney stones. Patients with nephrolithiasis often present with nonspecific symptoms, for example, nausea and vomiting. Patients may also present with hematuria, or blood in the urine. This is because the stones can disrupt the epithelium in the ureter, and that results in bleeding. But the key here is that on urinalysis, there are free RBCs with normal morphology. Now the term free RBCs means that individual red blood cells can be seen on microscopic analysis. But what is meant by free? Well, free RBCs just means intact, round RBCs that are individual and not clumped together. If they are clumped together, that would make you think of destruction of the red blood cells and would point you towards another pathology, for example, nephritis. But free RBCs does not imply the red blood cell destruction shows that they're intact, and so this is what you would expect with a kidney stone. After all, the kidney stone, unlike nephritis, is not damaging the nephron or the glomerulus. Instead, free red blood cells are more indicative of damage to the urinary tract. Now patients with nephrolithiasis also experience unilateral waxing and waning pain. This is often referred to as colicky pain. Now the location of the pain differs depending on where the obstruction occurs. For example, if the obstruction is at the ureto-pelvic junction, the patient's pain will be in the flank or upper abdominal region. If the obstruction is at the uretero-vesicle junction, so where the ureter meets the bladder, then the patient's pain will be in the lower abdominal region. Looking at this diagram makes that idea pretty logical. If the stone obstructs flow at the junction between the kidney and the ureter, so right here, then the patient will get flank pain. If the stone obstructs flow at the urethra and the bladder junction, then the patient will have lower abdominal pain. But again, in either of these two places, the pain will still be waxing and waning. Lastly, let's focus on the types of stones. There are four types of stones you need to know about. Calcium stones, up in the top. Ammonium magnesium phosphate stones. Uric acid stones. And cysteine stones. We'll start with calcium stones. Calcium stones are due to the precipitation of calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate. And these calcium stones are the most common type. And they're often seen in adults. Now calcium oxalate stones are radio opaque, meaning they can be seen on x-ray and they often look like envelopes on histology. Now calcium phosphate stones are also radio opaque, but they're prism shaped on histology. What causes these calcium stones? Well, hypercalciuria, or increased urine calcium. Hypercalcemia, for example, hypercalcemia caused by hyperparathyroidism. Or hypocitrature, so low urine citrate levels. Now hypocitrature occurs as a complication of distal renal tubular acidosis. In this condition, tubular citrate reabsorption is increased, leading to decreased citrate in the urine. And that's a problem because citrate normally binds calcium. And by doing that, citrate would prevent calcium from precipitating and forming a stone. So low urinary citrate means calcium is more free to bind to oxalate or phosphate and form stones. And sometimes it's just idiopathic. We don't really know what is causing the calcium stones. You treat calcium stones with hydrochlorothiazide, which is a thiazide diuretic. And in our renal pharmacology chapter, we have a story on thiazides and how they're used in the treatment of calcium stones. The reason this drug is helpful is because it causes calcium reabsorption, effectively removing the calcium from the urine filtrate and returning it to the serum. So by increasing calcium reabsorption, it's effectively preventing the calcium from precipitating into stones. Here's an image of calcium oxalate crystals on microscopy. Notice the square envelope-shaped crystals throughout. If envelope-shaped crystals are mentioned in a vignette, be sure to think about calcium oxalate stones. Next, let's discuss ammonium-magnesium-phosphate stones. These are also known as struvite stones, and they're associated with recurrent UTIs. So if a patient presents with colicky pain and has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections, you should definitely consider ammonium-magnesium-phosphate stones as a potential cause. Now, these stones can have staghorn calculi. This is a large stone that fills the renal calyces and the renal pelvis. And by precipitating here and forming this staghorn calculi, the collecting system of the kidney is effectively obstructed. This can lead to atrophy of the renal parenchyma. We'll look at an image of a staghorn calculus in a bit. Now, these struvite stones are also radio-opaque, and they look like little coffins on histology. And these are caused by infections with urease-expressing bacteria. And the ones you really need to know about are protease and klebsiella. Let's discuss why the urease is so important here. Let's say this is the lumen of the nephron, and within it, we'll have the filtrate. Now, urea is a substance in the filtrate. And klebsiella and protease produce urease. And this urease will hydrolyze the urea into ammonia. And this is the important part. Ammonia will increase urine pH, making it easier for ammonium-magnesium-phosphate salts to precipitate and form stones. Now, ammonium-magnesium-phosphate stones are treated by surgical removal of the staghorn calculus. And treatment should also eliminate the infection that's causing the stones in order to prevent recurrence. Here's an x-ray from a patient with a staghorn calculus. This is a characteristic image, and images like this are often used on exam in order to point towards ammonium-magnesium-phosphate stones, or struvite stones. Again, these stones are caused by urease-positive organisms, such as protease or klebsiella. Here's an image of a struvite stone on microscopy. Notice the rectangular, coffin-lid-shaped crystals throughout. This is characteristic of struvite stones in the urine. So, if you see coffin-lid crystals, or if they are mentioned or described in a vignette, think about ammonium-magnesium-phosphate stones, or struvite stones.
